extracted.intended_audience: writers (independent and traditionally published) working under United States copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for writers about how U.S. copyright works, what protections are automatic vs. registered, how to use others' material, and realistic enforcement options for independent and traditionally published authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic copyright upon fixation
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1989, the author of a work is automatically granted a copyright to that work. The act of finishing a work that’s fixed in a tangible medium—i.e. on paper or in a digital file—automatically grants you a copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't have to include a notice, send paperwork to a government office, or be published to have copyright; the mere existence of a finished, fixed work confers copyright protection. For most writers this automatic protection is sufficient unless you plan to sue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration required before filing a federal lawsuit
rubrics_metrics.description: If you ever want to bring a lawsuit and think you’ll need federal copyright protection, you are required to have registered your work with the US Copyright Office first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration alerts federal court that you claim authorship on a certain date. Without registration you cannot file a federal copyright infringement suit. Registration is a separate concept from automatic copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include copyright notice when you may sue (recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: If filing a lawsuit is something you can imagine yourself doing, it’s recommended that you include a copyright notice in your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copyright notice prevents an infringer from claiming they didn’t know the work was copyrighted. If you aren’t going to sue, a notice has little practical advantage; including one is largely 'warm and fuzzy' rather than legally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical decision rule for registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Register your copyright only if you have the resources, the time, and the willingness to file and pursue a copyright lawsuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because lawsuits are expensive and time-consuming, registration is recommended only when you can picture financing and pursuing legal action; otherwise automatic copyright protection is usually adequate for most writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor Man’s Copyright is ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Poor Man’s Copyright' — mailing yourself a sealed copy in an envelope — is a myth and not a substitute for proper registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sealed-envelope scheme will not substitute for registration in court; a correctly registered copyright is a required prerequisite to filing a lawsuit. Relying on a 'poor man’s copyright' is an anti-pattern if you expect legal enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for addressing infringement (independent writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent writers’ practical options if someone uses your work without permission: (1) contact the infringer and ask for removal or compensation, (2) contact the hosting service and submit a DMCA takedown request, (3) bring a lawsuit (if registered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option 1 is low-cost but may fail; Option 2 is low-risk but may not recover damages and can be countered by an infringement claim; Option 3 can recover damages but requires registration and significant legal costs. Independent writers should evaluate cost/benefit realistically before suing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers generally enforce copyright for traditionally published writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors signed with big publishers usually have the publisher’s legal team to advise and enforce copyright, making enforcement effectively the publisher’s concern rather than the author’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If traditionally published, you often needn't personally pursue enforcement; the publisher’s resources make enforcement realistic. This creates disparity between independent and traditionally published authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission required to use excerpts of copyrighted works
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re using an excerpt from a work created by someone else in your own writing—even just a sentence—and you’re not writing commentary, criticism, a news report, a scholarly report, or a parody, and the work is not in the public domain, then you must get permission from the author or rightsholder first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, get permission. Even single sentences, song lyrics, or poetry require permission unless a clear exception applies. Don’t rely on informal rationales; obtain rights or clearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use categories that may permit use without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions that can allow use without permission include writing that is commentary, criticism, a news report, a scholarly report, or a parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair use is fuzzy and judged case-by-case by courts; being unsure about whether your use qualifies is risky. Don’t attempt technicalities if your defense would depend on a judge’s subjective assessment—get permission if uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Very old work that is in the public domain may be used by anybody without permission because its copyright has expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining public domain status can be tricky; due to changes in law, most U.S. work produced after 1927 will not enter the public domain in your lifetime. Verify public domain status before relying on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters and settings can be protected (derivative works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects intangible elements like characters and settings; using established characters/settings (e.g., Star Wars) without permission can create an illegal derivative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fan fiction using copyrighted characters/settings is often technically infringing—even if rightsholders usually do not sue—so risk remains. Parody/criticism may be exceptions but are judged case-by-case; don’t assume you’re safe without permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical posture: don’t obsess over copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: For most writers composing entirely original work, copyright is one of the very last things they should be concerned about; enforcement realities mean most creators need not obsess about copyright protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given rarity of plagiarism and practical enforcement costs, focus on craft (plot, characters) rather than obsessing over copyright minutiae. If you have a serious situation, consult an intellectual property attorney.
